lead: Every processor designer faces one question: how much work should a single instruction do? CISC (complex instruction set computer) packs a lot of work into each instruction, so programs stay short. RISC (reduced instruction set computer) keeps instructions small and regular, so the hardware can overlap them and compilers can schedule them. The 8086 and 8051 are CISC-like; ARM is RISC. The choice shapes instruction length, addressing modes, register count and control logic, and it decides how easily the CPU can be pipelined.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for the fetch-decode-execute cycle and Chapter 1.2 for how the CPU reads instructions from memory.

blocks.text: CISC makes each instruction do a lot of work. RISC keeps each instruction small and pushes the work into software. Both are answers to the same question: given a fixed number of transistors, do you build complex instructions or a fast simple pipeline?

CISC grew up when memory was costly. A program that occupies fewer bytes needs less memory and fewer instruction fetches, so designers packed work into single instructions: add a memory word to a register, auto-increment a pointer, move a whole string. The 8086 is the classic case. Its instructions are 1 to 6 bytes long, it offers many addressing modes, and it has only eight general 16-bit registers (AX, BX, CX, DX, SI, DI, BP, SP). The 8051 is CISC-like in the same way.

RISC took the opposite bet: keep instructions so simple and regular that hardware can overlap them. ARM is the common example. Instructions are 4 bytes in ARM state, there are 16 general 32-bit registers, and only load and store instructions touch memory. Every arithmetic instruction works register to register. Because all instructions are the same length, the address of the next instruction is known before the current one is decoded, which makes pipelining natural.

Control logic is the last difference. A microcoded CPU holds a small internal program called microcode in a ROM inside the chip; each machine instruction becomes a sequence of micro-operations. Complex instructions are easier to build this way, so CISC uses microcode. RISC uses hardwired control: fixed logic gates decode the few instruction formats directly, which is faster and leaves chip area for pipeline registers.

sections.h3: The two styles side by side

blocks.text: Two rows need care. Load-store means arithmetic can only read and write registers; a value must be brought in by a load and written back by a store. This costs extra instructions but keeps every arithmetic instruction the same shape and the same duration. Cycles per instruction, written CPI, is the average number of clock cycles one instruction takes.

The compiler matters more on RISC. With fixed formats and few modes, a compiler can pick registers, reorder independent instructions and fill pipeline slots. On CISC the microcode already sequences the complicated steps, so the compiler has less to do but also less freedom.

sections.h3: Which one is faster? Count cycles, not CPI

blocks.text: A RISC instruction usually takes fewer cycles, but a task usually needs more RISC instructions. Neither number alone decides speed. Multiply them.

blocks.where: IC is the instruction count for the whole program (a pure number); CPI is the average clock cycles per instruction; Total cycles is the number of clock periods the program needs.

blocks.text: Time = IC × CPI × T_clk = (IC × CPI) ÷ f
blocks.where: T_clk is the clock period in seconds; f is the clock frequency in hertz, f = 1 ÷ T_clk.

blocks.text: So a machine with CPI = 1.2 can still lose to one with CPI = 4 if it executes far more instructions. The worked example below uses exactly this comparison. Notice also that the answer depends on the program, the compiler and the clock frequency, so no design wins every time. Modern x86 chips translate complex instructions into simple internal operations before executing them, and ARM has added some multi-step instructions, which shows the two ideas have moved closer.

figure.caption: Instruction set design splits into two branches. The CISC branch keeps many addressing modes and microcoded control; the RISC branch keeps load-store access and a pipeline-friendly fixed format.

spec.aria: A tree divides instruction set design into CISC, with variable length, many addressing modes and microcode, and RISC, with fixed length, load-store instructions and pipelining.

examples.question: A CISC CPU has 120 instructions and averages 4 clock cycles per instruction. A RISC CPU has 40 instructions and averages 1.2 clock cycles per instruction. A given program needs 10⁶ CISC instructions, or 1.4 × 10⁶ RISC instructions when compiled for the RISC machine. Both CPUs run at the same clock frequency. Find the clock cycles each machine needs and the ratio of RISC time to CISC time.
steps: CISC instruction count IC = 10⁶ instructions, CISC CPI = 4 cycles per instruction.
RISC instruction count IC = 1.4 × 10⁶ instructions, RISC CPI = 1.2 cycles per instruction.
Same clock frequency f means time = cycles ÷ f, so the time ratio equals the cycle ratio.
The RISC program runs in 42 % of the CISC time, so it is about 2.38 times faster here, even though it executes 1.4 times as many instructions.
examples.answer: CISC needs 4 × 10⁶ cycles, RISC needs 1.68 × 10⁶ cycles, and the RISC time is 0.42 of the CISC time at the same clock frequency.
examples.check:
cisc_ic = 1_000_000
cisc_cpi = 4.0
risc_ic = 1_400_000
risc_cpi = 1.2
cisc_cycles = cisc_ic * cisc_cpi
risc_cycles = risc_ic * risc_cpi
ratio = risc_cycles / cisc_cycles
print(cisc_cycles)
print(risc_cycles)
print(ratio)

traps: Comparing CPI alone. RISC usually has lower CPI but a larger instruction count; only IC × CPI gives the cycles.
Reading 'reduced' as 'fewer instructions executed'. RISC reduces the instruction set, not the program length; its programs are usually longer.
Mixing up the two control styles. Microcode is an internal ROM program inside the CPU; it is not the user's program in main memory.
Forgetting what load-store forbids. A load-store machine cannot add a memory operand straight into a register; you need a load, an add and possibly a store.
Claiming one style always wins. Workload, compiler and clock frequency all shift the answer; the examiner wants the cycle calculation, not a slogan.

quiz.q: Expand CISC and RISC, and state in one line what each style does with instruction complexity.
quiz.a: CISC is complex instruction set computer: few instructions, each doing a lot of work. RISC is reduced instruction set computer: many simple, regular instructions, each doing one small job.

quiz.q: Which of the 8086 and ARM is CISC and which is RISC? Give one supporting fact for each.
quiz.a: 8086 is CISC: variable-length instructions of 1 to 6 bytes with many addressing modes and memory operands. ARM is RISC: fixed 4-byte instructions, 16 general registers, load-store memory access.

quiz.q: Why does variable instruction length make pipelining harder?
quiz.a: The pipeline must fetch the next instruction before the current one is fully decoded. With variable length, the next address depends on the current instruction's size, so fetch and decode become serial and the pipeline may stall. Fixed length lets the next address be computed immediately.

quiz.q: Why did early CISC designs try to reduce program size, and why does that argument matter less today?
quiz.a: Memory was expensive and small, so shorter programs saved cost and reduced instruction fetches from slow memory. Today memory is cheap and large, and cache plus wide fetch make code size less critical, so pipeline speed matters more.

quiz.q: A CISC CPU runs a task in 2 × 10⁶ instructions at CPI 3. A RISC CPU runs the same task in 2.8 × 10⁶ instructions at CPI 1.15. Both run at the same clock. Find the cycles for each and the RISC/CISC time ratio.
quiz.a: CISC cycles = 2 × 10⁶ × 3 = 6 × 10⁶. RISC cycles = 2.8 × 10⁶ × 1.15 = 3.22 × 10⁶. Ratio = 3.22 × 10⁶ ÷ 6 × 10⁶ = 0.5367. The RISC program takes about 0.54 of the CISC time.

quiz.q: A marketing sheet says a new core has CPI = 1.0 and is therefore the fastest. Explain what extra information you need before accepting the claim.
quiz.a: CPI alone says nothing about total time. You need the instruction count the same program needs on each machine, the clock frequency, and cycles = IC × CPI. Time = (IC × CPI) ÷ f. A CPI of 1.0 with twice the instructions and half the clock can be much slower.

quiz.q: A compiler for a CISC machine almost never emits the complex multi-step instructions. What happens to the CISC advantage, and what does that suggest about the two styles?
quiz.a: The advantage shrinks. The CPU still pays for microcode and decode logic that the program rarely uses, while a simple hardwired RISC core of the same area could run at a higher clock. It suggests the styles converge: keep a simple fast core and let software do the work.

quiz.q: What does load-store mean, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: Only load and store instructions move data between memory and registers; all arithmetic works register to register. The cost is extra instructions and extra register pressure, because a value must be loaded, used and stored back.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real x86 processors decode complex instructions into small internal operations that look much like RISC instructions, so the boundary has blurred in production silicon. ARM dominates phones and embedded boards, and the open RISC-V instruction set is now taught and used in research and startups. Compiler work on register allocation and instruction scheduling matters most on load-store machines. Search for 'micro-ops', 'RISC-V ISA specification' and 'ARM Cortex-M architecture' to go further; Unit 6 covers ARM in detail.
